concept.title: Capability ladder
concept.fires-when: Scoping any initiative; answering "what's next" at session start; suspecting false-done.
concept.md: One capability per initiative, one falsifiable exit per capability, tiers per increment: T0 substrate missing → T1 present but not wired → T2 wired but not tested → T3 tested but not shipped → T4 shipped but not adopted. The ladder is O(1) orientation — next work is always the lowest tier whose exit is not provably green — and a false-done detector: closure-orientation cannot mask incomplete work when every tier has a command-verifiable exit.

concept.title: Initiatives and increments
concept.fires-when: Breaking an objective into sessions of work; sizing what one session may promise.
concept.md: An initiative carries one falsifiable goal and a single success metric — "fix class X at root Y" form (constitution §fix-the-class). Increments are the rungs it ships on: each is a vertical slice that leaves the system whole and provably one tier higher, never a horizontal layer that leaves everything half-wired. An increment that cannot state its exit check is not yet an increment; it is an intention.

concept.title: Unison — never compromise one part to fix another
concept.fires-when: Any fix spanning systems or layers; before implementing a ratified design; when a green check feels too easy.
concept.md: Every session moves the system forward in unison: a change that fixes its target while fragmenting the whole fails, even when its code is clean, reviewed, and verified. Run the premise-check BEFORE executing: "which engine already owns this responsibility?" A parallel mechanism beside an existing owner is fragmentation with extra steps. Distrust the green live-proof that only shows the symptom gone; trade-offs that bend another component get an explicit follow-up task, never silence.

concept.title: Ratified ≠ implemented; implemented ≠ accepted
concept.fires-when: Closing any phase, task, or fix; reading a design doc that says "X happens"; inheriting a prompt's claims.
concept.md: Two distinct gaps, both fatal to trust. A ratified decision is prose recording intent — grep the implied code path and run the live operation before treating it as built. And shipped code that works is still not accepted until the class has a structural guard: ask "if we removed this code, does the class reappear?" — if yes, the fix is isolated, not accepted; it needs a gate, a type, a contract, or a check that makes recurrence impossible.

concept.title: Design-artifact set — the ready-to-start gate
concept.fires-when: Any work spanning more than one layer or component; before dispatching builders.
concept.md: No implementation begins until the artifact set exists: solution design, implementation design, diagram, and contract — design-reviewed and operator-ratified. The same set gates ready-to-close. Sizing is proportional to scope (a small fix still surfaces design + diagram, briefly), but the gate itself never waives: it pays for itself the first time review catches a false invariant before code exists.

concept.title: Bounded context and ubiquitous language
concept.fires-when: Organizing domains; naming things; deciding where work or data belongs; noticing the same word meaning two things.
concept.md: A domain is a DDD bounded context: a boundary inside which every term has exactly one agreed meaning (the ubiquitous language) and one owning team. Boundaries are structural, not tags — things do not migrate casually across them, and a domain that accepts everything is a dumping ground that defeats the purpose. In the substrate itself, domains scope claims, lessons, and buckets; in systems you build, they scope ownership and governance.

concept.title: Published language and semantic contracts
concept.fires-when: Two components or products sharing data about the same entity; any breaking-change dispute; coupling decisions.
concept.md: A domain publishes a canonical definition of each shared entity; consumers couple to declared semantic intent ("requires: customer_classification"), never to internals like column names. The contract is validated structurally at deploy/merge time and evaluated on upstream change as holds, stale, or broken — broken blocks, with an event, not a surprise six months later. This is the use-promise (−) made mechanical: downstream relies only on what upstream promised, and the platform enforces the reliance.

concept.title: Architectural quantum
concept.fires-when: Drawing deployment or ownership boundaries; deciding what "one unit" of a system is.
concept.md: The smallest independently deployable unit with high functional cohesion, carrying everything its function needs: logic, contract, metadata, infrastructure declaration. "Independent" means an independent lifecycle and ownership — not necessarily isolated runtime. In socom, the promise is the quantum of work; in data platforms, the data product is the quantum of architecture; both compose into aggregates without surrendering autonomy.

concept.title: The published gate — safe-by-construction at the right altitude
concept.fires-when: Designing any validation; deciding WHERE a failure should surface; consumer-facing errors that trace to producer omissions.
concept.md: Move validation to the altitude where the person who can fix it meets it: a product missing classification fails at the owner's publish step with an actionable message — never as a consumer's read-time 500. By the time anything is visible to a consumer it is safe-to-share by construction. Generalized: every gate should fire at the desk of whoever owns the fix, as early as that desk allows (shift-left applied to governance).

concept.title: Fail-closed vs fail-open — choose the posture per concern
concept.fires-when: Designing any failure path, fallback, degradation, or health check.
concept.md: Degradation is designed, never discovered. Security concerns (auth, masking, classification) fail CLOSED: refuse rather than degrade, a 404 over an unmasked row. Quality concerns (freshness, completeness) fail OPEN: serve the previous good version with degradation metadata rather than nothing. Every external dependency names its fallback at design time; a dependency without a declared posture is an undesigned outage.

concept.title: Falsifiable success metrics
concept.fires-when: Writing any goal, contract, exit criterion, or "definition of done".
concept.md: "How will we know?" must answer with a command and an expected output — "when [command] returns [result]" — never with "looks good" or "feels right". If the success of work cannot be falsified, the work cannot be promised, assessed, or handed off; reframe until it can. This is the doctrine that makes every other gate possible.
